newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Dutch run into row over Nigerian invitation.
newsitem.headline: Dutch run into row over Nigerian invitation.

text.p: The Dutch government, apparently flouting an EU ban on granting visas to members of Nigeria's government, ran into a political row in Brussels on Thursday.

The Netherlands, which holds the presidency of the EU, invited Nigeria to attend a meeting in Maastricht of government leaders from the 15-member EU bloc and its 70 partners in Africa, Caribbean and Pacific (ACP).
The Dutch foreign ministry said the visa restrictions applied only to "Nigerian authorities travelling to Europe for private reasons."

But members of the European Parliament protested that the invitation broke the EU's embargo on Nigeria, introduced last year after the executions of Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other human rights activists.

"It is appalling that...at a time when no progress has been made on human rights or progress towards democracy by (General Sani) Abacha's junta, the EU is giving credibility to the regime in Lagos and breaking the (sanctions) agreed after the executions," British Socialist Glenys Kinnock said in a statement.

A spokesman for the Dutch foreign ministry said the boycott was not an end in itself and was not intended to hinder next month's important political discussions on the future of relations between the EU and the ACP states.
"Nigeria is a prominent member of the ACP group. Without Nigeria, the talks between the EU and the ACP would be less significant," he said.
He said the decision to lift the visa restrictions had been taken after consultation with the European Commission, the EU's executive arm.

But a spokesman for Joao de Deus Pinheiro, the commissioner responsible for EU links with the ACP states, many of which are former European colonies, told reporters Pinheiro was not aware of the decision.

Parliamentary deputies from the EU and ACP states, meeting in Brussels, were due on Thursday to adopt a resolution accusing Nigeria of continuing human rights violations and urging the EU to impose tighter sanctions, including an oil embargo, until the abuses stopped and Lagos introduced genuine democratic reforms.
